doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Getting the 'Invasion of the Body Snatchers' score
summary: Philip Kaufman wanted him; he convinced producer Bob Solo and took a low offer that became well paid thanks to doubling.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Okay. Your work, composing work, in addition to “Quiet Now” of course, has appeared in some interesting places, including “Sesame Street” and “The Invasion of the Body Snatchers.” How did that film come about?

The film opportunity came about through a back door, sort of analogous to the John Hammond story. It turns out that Phillip Kaufman, the director who made “Invasion of the Body Snatchers,” was from Chicago and had heard me play years earlier, liked my playing, and had it in his head someday he wanted me to do a jazz score for one of his movies. So when “Invasion of the Body Snatchers” was just in the formative stages on the screenplay board, he called me and asked me if I would be interested in it, and at that time the protagonist, played by Donald Sutherland, was going to be an avocational jazz man. And so it was going to be very easy for that to be the legitimacy for a jazz score. But then as the script evolved he went from being a jazz player to a deputy public health officer, and now they wanted a twentieth century classical musical score and electronics and everything. And I had no established credentials for doing that at all. So I had to convince first Phil that I could do it, and then a much tougher sell was to convince his producer, Bob Solo, that I could do it. I think if I had been in Solo’s position, I wouldn’t have taken a chance on me. This was then a quite expensive movie, five or six million dollars in 1978 was significant money. And I think I would have been tempted to go with an established pro who had credentials where I wouldn’t have to wonder whether this guy’s going to mess up the film. But Phil was so adamant about wanting me, and then when I was — I think Bob Solo’s sort of graceful way of hoping I wouldn’t do it was to make me such an insulting offer that I would walk away in a huff. But I wanted to do this. I was willing to do it for nothing, for the experience. So —

I called his bluff. I took it. And then it turned out because of the way the movie was constructed and all the different instruments I was playing, I was playing all kinds of electronic keyboard instruments and all this stuff and just the way you legitimately bill for services in union contracts, I ended up —
